paragraphs: Collaborative filtering uses patterns in user ratings to make recommendations. This paper develops a framework based on restricted Boltzmann machines that accounts for relationships among both users and items. Earlier RBM approaches emphasized correlations between item ratings; the proposed hybrid framework brings user-user correlations into the same model. Its non-IID framing treats these dependencies as information to model.

The framework also changes how ratings are represented. It uses real-valued visible variables instead of multinomial variables, allowing the model to take advantage of ratings having a natural order. The authors additionally explore a bootstrapping strategy that combines observed training data with data generated by the model itself.

Evaluation on the MovieLens datasets containing 100,000 and one million ratings shows performance competitive with the best previously proposed approaches. This supports the combined framework as a promising recommendation method. The abstract presents bootstrapping as an explored possibility, however, and does not attribute the overall result to any single modification.
icml-2013-a-non-iid-framework-for-collab.tldr: A hybrid RBM recommendation framework models relationships among both users and items and achieves competitive results on two MovieLens datasets.

paragraphs: Binary classification assigns each example to one of two classes. The 0–1 loss measures whether that assignment is wrong, making it a direct expression of classification error. The paper contrasts its robustness to outliers with the sensitivity of convex losses, which are attractive because efficient methods can find their global optima.

Directly optimizing 0–1 loss is NP-hard, but the authors investigate whether useful approximate solutions are nevertheless practical. They explore branch-and-bound search, combinatorial search, and coordinate descent applied to smooth, differentiable relaxations. These approaches provide different ways to work with an objective that does not have the convenient optimization structure of a convex loss.

In the reported experiments, the proposed methods perform at least as well as logistic regression, support vector machines, and the Bayes point machine, with a clear advantage when outliers are present. The finding challenges the practical dismissal of direct 0–1 optimization. It does not remove the underlying computational hardness; it shows that approximate optimization can be effective in the evaluated settings.
icml-2013-algorithms-for-direct-01-loss-.tldr: Practical approximations to direct 0–1 loss optimization match competing classifiers in experiments and offer an advantage with outliers.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best option in a stochastic multi-armed bandit, where trying an option produces uncertain evidence about its quality. The central resource is the number of arm pulls needed to make that identification. Existing upper and lower bounds differed by a multiplicative logarithmic factor, which can become consequential for large problems.

The authors introduce two parameter-free algorithms for two versions of the task. One starts with a desired confidence level; the other starts with a fixed budget of arm pulls. They prove upper bounds whose remaining gap from the lower bound is only doubly logarithmic in the problem parameters.

These results bring the theoretical cost of exploration closer to the known limits without claiming to close the gap completely. Experiments support the analysis: the proposed approach outperforms the state of the art in the reported comparisons and scales better as problem size increases. The contribution combines stronger guarantees with empirical evidence that the improvement matters as exploration problems grow.
icml-2013-almost-optimal-exploration-in-.tldr: Two best-arm identification algorithms reduce the gap to known exploration lower bounds from logarithmic to doubly logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: A classifier's usefulness can depend on how much computation or feature acquisition it requires when making a prediction. Search and spam filtering need quick decisions, while medical diagnosis can involve expensive features. The paper treats this test-time expense as a central design concern, alongside the ability to classify inputs.

The proposed algorithm, Anytime Feature Representations, addresses the trade-off through the data representation. Its key choice is to make the representation account for evaluation cost, allowing a conventional classifier to acquire anytime behavior. This places the mechanism for managing test-time expense in the features supplied to the classifier.

The authors state that the approach can turn conventional classifiers, particularly support vector machines, into cost-sensitive anytime classifiers. Its significance is the combination of flexible evaluation with large-margin classification: a familiar classification approach can participate in a system designed around test-time resource constraints. The contribution described here is this representational route to combining the two capabilities.
icml-2013-anytime-representation-learnin.tldr: Anytime Feature Representations make conventional classifiers sensitive to test-time costs by addressing the trade-off in the data representation.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning needs to learn an environment model, a task that becomes difficult when observations occupy a large space. Factoring that space can divide model learning into smaller problems. The difficulty is that many decompositions may be available, and choosing a useful one can otherwise require extensive testing.

This paper introduces a family called recursively decomposable factorizations. Within that family, the authors show how to perform exact Bayesian inference efficiently. The accompanying guarantee places predictive performance close to that of the best factorization in the class, providing a principled way to handle uncertainty about how the observation space should be divided.

The comparison class is central to the result: the predictive guarantee is relative to the introduced family of factorizations. The authors also present empirical results across 20 Atari 2600 games to demonstrate the approach's strength. Together, the theoretical and empirical contributions address both the computational challenge of learning large environment models and the difficulty of selecting their structure.
icml-2013-bayesian-learning-of-recursive.tldr: Efficient exact Bayesian inference provides predictive performance close to the best recursively decomposable factorization of an environment.

paragraphs: Random forests have achieved practical success faster than the theory explaining their behavior has developed. This paper addresses that imbalance for online random forests. Its stated contribution is a consistency result, giving a theoretical basis for understanding a learning method whose practical use has run ahead of its mathematical analysis.

Consistency concerns the behavior of a learning procedure as the amount of available data grows. Its importance is that it connects learning from finite observations with a longer-run statistical objective. For online random forests, this directs attention to the learning procedure's behavior as observations accumulate, complementing the practical question of how well a forest works on a particular dataset.

The paper frames its result as a step toward narrowing the gap between theory and practice. That framing matters: the contribution is a mathematical justification for online random forests in the setting analyzed. It adds a form of evidence about learning behavior that practical success alone does not establish.
icml-2013-consistency-of-online-random-f.tldr: The paper establishes a consistency result for online random forests, helping connect their practical success with statistical theory.

paragraphs: When two entities look alike, their resemblance may reflect a real connection or an ordinary coincidence. This paper studies how to detect rare connected pairs across settings such as social analysis, fraud detection, and entity resolution. The central question is whether a similarity is surprising given how common the entities' characteristics are.

The authors propose a mixture model in which most entities arise independently, while a small number of pairs are constrained to resemble one another. A likelihood ratio identifies candidate links by balancing similarity against rarity. Consequently, the method can distinguish resemblance that is common in the population from resemblance that provides stronger evidence of a connection.

Within the proposed analysis, the likelihood-ratio method outperforms using similarity alone, although similarity remains surprisingly competitive for some parameter settings. Real-data applications detect twins from birth weights and re-identify phone users through distinctive usage patterns. These examples demonstrate how the same modeling idea can support different tasks involving unusually similar pairs.
icml-2013-copy-or-coincidence-a-model-fo.tldr: A mixture model detects rare linked pairs by weighing both their similarity and how unusual that similarity is.

paragraphs: Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis learns representations of two views of data so that the transformed views have strong linear correlation. Each transformation can be complex and nonlinear. Their parameters are learned jointly to maximize regularized total correlation, extending the aim of linear canonical correlation analysis to a more flexible representation family.

The paper positions DCCA as a parametric alternative to kernel canonical correlation analysis. It does not require an inner product, and the learned transformations can represent unseen instances without referring back to the training data. The authors also identify favorable scaling of training time with data size as an advantage of the parametric approach.

On two real-world datasets, DCCA learns representations with significantly higher correlation than those produced by CCA and KCCA. This finding directly supports its ability to capture shared variation between views. The paper additionally introduces a cube-root-based, non-saturating sigmoid function and suggests that it may have broader use in feedforward neural networks.
icml-2013-deep-canonical-correlation-ana.tldr: DCCA jointly learns nonlinear transformations of two data views, achieving higher representation correlation than CCA and KCCA on two datasets.

paragraphs: Tuning a physical controller can require expensive experiments, and an experiment may reveal only success or failure. The paper studies optimization under this stochastic binary feedback. Its objective is to obtain a strong controller after an offline training phase, so the value of an experiment comes from helping select the final controller.

The authors define this optimization problem and develop a Bayesian optimization framework using an adaptation of Gaussian processes for classification. This accommodates binary observations while supporting decisions about which controller settings to try next. They also propose an experiment-selection metric based on expected improvement, tailored to the success-or-failure setting.

The approach is demonstrated on synthetic problems and a real snake robot learning to cross an obstacle. These applications show how binary experimental feedback can guide controller optimization even when no graded performance measurement is observed. The paper's contribution is the combination of a problem formulation, a probabilistic modeling approach, and a criterion for selecting informative experiments.
icml-2013-expensive-function-optimizatio.tldr: A Bayesian optimization framework tunes expensive controllers using only stochastic success-or-failure observations.

paragraphs: An ontology specifies relationships among multiple outputs. This paper asks how such relationships can help learn several related classification tasks when the available data are primarily unlabeled. The motivation is that learning tasks together may provide information through their connections, even when direct examples of the correct outputs are scarce.

The authors introduce a theoretical model for studying this effect. Their analysis includes information-theoretic results and efficient algorithms, addressing both what information can support learning and how that information can be used computationally. In this setting, the ontology supplies structure that a large unlabeled data source can help make useful.

The strongest stated result is conditional: in some cases within the model, the ontology and a large unlabeled source are sufficient to learn a classification completely. This gives a precise sense in which relationships among outputs can carry substantial learning information. The result explains a possible source of ontologies' effectiveness without asserting that every ontology makes labeled data unnecessary.
icml-2013-exploiting-ontology-structures.tldr: A theoretical model shows that, in some cases, output relationships and abundant unlabeled data suffice to learn a classification completely.

paragraphs: Automatic image tagging assigns descriptive labels to images. Strong nearest-neighbor approaches improve retrieval accuracy by learning carefully chosen metric spaces, but their training and prediction can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces FastTag to retain competitive annotation quality while reducing those computational demands.

FastTag uses two simple linear mappings trained together through a convex objective with co-regularization. The shared loss couples the mappings, so the method's simplicity does not require learning them independently. Efficient closed-form updates make optimization inexpensive and allow the method to incorporate many image descriptors at relatively low cost.

Across several standard real-world benchmark datasets, FastTag matches the reported state of the art in tagging quality while reducing training and testing times by several orders of magnitude. The authors also report lower asymptotic complexity. The finding supports a substantial efficiency improvement in the evaluated tasks: jointly trained linear mappings can provide competitive tags without the computational expense associated with the compared methods.
icml-2013-fast-image-tagging-ae45e7e7eb.tldr: FastTag uses two jointly trained linear mappings to match benchmark tagging quality while greatly reducing training and prediction time.

paragraphs: Some estimation problems involve matrices with more than one useful kind of structure. This paper focuses on matrices that are both sparse and low rank: many entries are zero, while the matrix also has a compact underlying representation. The challenge is to design a regularizer that encourages these structural properties simultaneously.

The authors propose a new complexity index and a convex penalty that approximates it. The penalty can be expressed as the trace norm of a linear transformation of the matrix. This gives the joint structural preference a specific mathematical form while preserving convexity, making it suitable for a regularized estimation objective.

The theoretical analysis provides oracle inequalities and compressed sensing results supporting the quality of the resulting estimator. These guarantees connect the proposed regularizer to estimation and recovery performance under the analyzed conditions. The paper also supplies algorithms and numerical experiments, linking its regularizer design to computation. Its main contribution is a principled way to encourage multiple matrix structures within one convex penalty.
icml-2013-intersecting-singularities-for.tldr: A new convex regularizer jointly encourages sparsity and low rank, with theoretical estimation guarantees and supporting algorithms.

paragraphs: Ordinary cross-validation randomly distributes data points among test sets, implicitly treating the observations as exchangeable. That assumption can fail when data come from multiple sources, as in transfer learning. Source identity then matters to the evaluation, and practitioners commonly organize cross-validation to respect that structure.

The paper develops theory for this practice by introducing estimators of cross-validation variance. Variance describes the uncertainty surrounding an evaluation result, which is essential when deciding how confidently to interpret an apparent performance difference. The authors provide estimators for both the multiple-source setting and the standard setting with independent, identically distributed data.

The stated benefit is substantially more accurate confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for comparing algorithms. This shifts attention from obtaining a cross-validation score to assessing how reliable that score and its comparisons are. By accounting for source structure in the uncertainty calculation, the work supports more trustworthy interpretation of evaluations involving multiple data sources, while also improving uncertainty estimation in the standard setting.
icml-2013-multiple-source-cross-validati.tldr: New cross-validation variance estimators improve confidence intervals and algorithm comparisons for both multiple-source and standard IID data.

paragraphs: Constrained stochastic optimization commonly projects an updated solution back into the allowed domain at every iteration. That operation can dominate computation when the domain is complicated, such as the cone of positive semidefinite matrices. This paper asks whether strong convergence can be retained while performing far fewer projections.

The proposed algorithm combines mini-batches, extra-gradient steps, and epoch gradient descent to exploit smoothness and strong convexity. These properties are central assumptions of the result. Under them, the authors prove an optimal O(1/T) convergence rate using only O(log T) projections, with guarantees both in expectation and with high probability.

The significance is that the number of expensive feasibility operations grows only logarithmically with T while the stated convergence rate remains optimal. This targets a computational bottleneck that counting iterations alone can obscure. An empirical study supports the theoretical result, connecting the reduced projection requirement to observed behavior. The guarantee applies to the smooth, strongly convex setting analyzed in the paper.
icml-2013-o-logt-projections-for-stochas.tldr: For smooth, strongly convex objectives, the proposed stochastic optimizer achieves optimal O(1/T) convergence with only O(log T) projections.

paragraphs: Training deep and recurrent neural networks was considered extremely difficult with stochastic gradient descent and momentum. This paper examines the importance of two choices within that approach: how the network's parameters are initialized and how momentum changes during training. The authors use a carefully designed random initialization together with a slowly increasing momentum schedule.

With those choices, they train deep networks and recurrent networks on long-term-dependency datasets to performance levels previously reached only by Hessian-Free optimization. Both ingredients matter in the reported findings. Momentum does not rescue poorly initialized networks, and good initialization produces markedly worse results when momentum is absent or badly tuned.

The results suggest that poor initialization likely contributed to earlier failures to train these models from random starting points. They also show that carefully tuned momentum can handle the curvature difficulties encountered in the studied training objectives. The practical implication is that initialization and momentum scheduling can determine whether a comparatively simple optimization method is effective.
icml-2013-on-the-importance-of-initializ.tldr: Careful random initialization and slowly increasing momentum let stochastic gradient descent reach previously Hessian-Free-level performance on the studied networks.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, a prediction can assign several labels to one example. This paper compares two ways to optimize the F-measure for that task. A plug-in approach first learns a probabilistic model and then derives a prediction through a separate inference step. Structured loss minimization instead targets the measure during training.

The authors introduce a plug-in algorithm that uses a collection of multinomial regression models to estimate all parameters needed for a Bayes-optimal prediction. This separates learning the relevant probabilities from deciding which labels to output. They compare the method with structured support vector machines in both computational complexity and statistical consistency.

The main theoretical finding is that the proposed plug-in algorithm is consistent, whereas the SSVM approaches studied are not. This distinguishes their long-run statistical behavior, beyond whether their training objectives appear directly aligned with the evaluation measure. A large experimental study also reports benefits for the proposed algorithm, supporting its practical value alongside the consistency result.
icml-2013-optimizing-the-f-measure-in-mu.tldr: A multinomial-regression plug-in method for multi-label F-measure optimization is consistent, unlike the structured SVM approaches examined.

paragraphs: In cost-sensitive multiclass classification, prediction mistakes can have different costs. Obtaining labels can also be expensive, motivating algorithms that choose which examples need annotation. This paper develops selective sampling methods that process a stream of data and request labels for only a subset of the examples.

The analysis studies regret and label complexity under a generalized linear model for label generation. These quantities capture prediction performance and the number of requested labels. A margin condition determines how much active learning helps: the advantage over passive learning can range from no gain to an exponentially large gain.

This range is a central finding because selective querying does not provide the same benefit in every setting. The paper also supplies a safety guarantee intended to guard against mismatch between the assumed model and the data. Numerical simulations report low regret with few label requests, supporting the methods' ability to combine selective annotation with effective cost-sensitive prediction in the evaluated settings.
icml-2013-selective-sampling-algorithms-.tldr: Streaming selective-sampling algorithms achieve margin-dependent labeling gains for cost-sensitive prediction, with a safeguard against model mismatch.

paragraphs: Kernel methods work with functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. Basic operations can produce a function outside the desired space; multiplying two RKHS functions is one example. This paper develops a general framework for approximating such operations while guaranteeing that the resulting function belongs to a chosen target RKHS.

The framework covers operations including multiplication, composition, changes of measure, and conditional expectation. An adjoint-based transformation turns the approximation task into regression. The regression takes place in a vector-valued RKHS whose elements are continuous linear operators mapping functions from the input space to the target space.

Convex constraints on these operators allow important requirements, such as a density being positive almost everywhere, to be enforced or approximated. Operators can also be composed to perform more complex tasks, including the sum rule and kernelized approximate Bayesian inference. The paper reports state-of-the-art convergence rates for these applications, showing how a common mathematical construction can support both basic operations and larger inference procedures.
icml-2013-smooth-operators-28004be453.tldr: Smooth operators approximate mathematical operations within a target RKHS and compose into kernel-based inference procedures.

paragraphs: A sparse Gaussian conditional random field models a high-dimensional distribution of outputs given inputs. The paper studies this discriminative extension of sparse inverse covariance estimation, using convex methods to learn it. Its motivation is that earlier work offered limited theoretical analysis and struggled to solve large instances of the optimization problem.

The authors develop a second-order active-set method and report that it is several orders of magnitude faster than earlier optimization approaches for this problem. They also improve the theoretical bounds, obtaining convergence rates that depend logarithmically on data dimension. These contributions address computation and statistical analysis as distinct parts of making the model useful at scale.

The method is applied to large-scale energy forecasting and achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on two real-world tasks. The application results show that the model and solver can support demanding prediction problems. Taken together, the work strengthens an existing modeling approach through faster optimization, sharper theory, and evidence from practical forecasting.
icml-2013-sparse-gaussian-conditional-ra.tldr: A faster solver and stronger theory make sparse Gaussian conditional random fields effective for large-scale energy forecasting.

paragraphs: In nonparametric regression, choosing a kernel's structural form is an important modeling decision that can be difficult to make systematically. This paper turns that choice into a search problem. It defines candidate structures by adding and multiplying a small collection of base kernels, creating a compositional space of possible models.

The proposed method searches this space in a way the authors describe as mirroring scientific discovery. The search concerns the form of the kernel itself, making structural choices part of learning. The resulting structures can often separate a fitted function into interpretable components, helping explain the patterns represented by the model.

The learned structures can also enable long-range extrapolation on time-series datasets. Across a variety of prediction tasks, the search method outperforms many commonly used kernels and kernel-combination methods. These findings support systematic kernel construction as useful for prediction and interpretation. The interpretability and extrapolation claims are possibilities demonstrated by the approach, rather than guarantees for every learned structure.
icml-2013-structure-discovery-in-nonpara.tldr: Searching over sums and products of base kernels discovers structures that can improve prediction, interpretation, and time-series extrapolation.

paragraphs: Data arranged in a matrix can contain dependencies both among observations and among features. Treating observations as independent can miss part of this structure, but freely modeling both kinds of relationship creates a large number of parameters. This paper introduces the bigraphical lasso to represent these dependencies more economically.

The estimator learns precision matrices for matrix-normal models using a structure based on the Cartesian product of graphs. That graph construction provides a way to organize the two types of partial correlation together. The authors identify useful properties for regression, sparsity, and interpretation, making the structural assumption part of the model's appeal.

To manage parameter growth, the method applies L1 penalties and uses a flip-flop fitting algorithm. The resulting computation involves a linear number of lasso regressions. This connects the structured estimation problem to repeated sparse regression problems. The contribution is a model and estimation strategy for capturing dependencies across both dimensions of a data matrix while controlling model complexity.
icml-2013-the-bigraphical-lasso-a6df9916.tldr: The bigraphical lasso models dependencies among both observations and features using graph-product structure and sparse estimation.

paragraphs: Cross-entropy optimization searches by maintaining a distribution over candidate solutions. It repeatedly evaluates sampled candidates and shifts the distribution toward a selected percentage of the highest-scoring ones. This paper examines what that percentage-based selection actually optimizes when evaluations are noisy, as they often are in control and decision-making environments.

The authors show that ordinary cross-entropy optimization targets a quantile metric in these settings, rather than expected utility. That distinction matters because favoring a particular part of the outcome distribution is different from favoring average performance. An optimization procedure can therefore appear appropriate while pursuing a criterion different from the intended objective.

The paper proposes Proportional CE, a variant that effectively optimizes expected value. Experiments using variants of established noisy environments show that it can replace ordinary CE and can improve solution quality. The result identifies both an objective mismatch in the original procedure and a practical alternative when expected performance is the desired criterion.
icml-2013-the-cross-entropy-method-optim.tldr: In noisy environments, standard cross-entropy optimization targets quantiles; Proportional CE instead targets expected value and can improve solutions.

paragraphs: Temporal models can include fixed parameters that affect transitions at every time step. Bayesian inference must learn those parameters alongside the evolving system. The paper describes difficulties with particle filters in this setting and notes that Gibbs-based parameter sampling can become more expensive as the observation sequence grows.

Storvik's filter can avoid that growing per-sample cost in some cases by incrementally updating exact sufficient statistics. The authors connect this method to a Kalman filter operating in parameter space and establish more general conditions for its applicability. This connection supplies a basis for extending the approach beyond the cases handled by exact updates.

Drawing on the extended Kalman filter analogy, the paper develops a Taylor approximation to the parameter posterior. The approximation makes Storvik's method applicable to a broader class of models and receives both theoretical and experimental analysis. Experiments on synthetic examples and real applications show improvements over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of this extension for sequential parameter inference.
icml-2013-the-extended-parameter-filter-.tldr: A Kalman-filter connection and Taylor posterior approximation extend Storvik's parameter filtering method to a broader class of temporal models.

paragraphs: Selecting the best fixed-size subset of alternatives becomes difficult when information about their quality is noisy. Racing algorithms address such problems through adaptive sampling. This paper considers a setting in which the available evidence consists of pairwise preferences: observations compare two alternatives rather than supply a numerical quality measurement for each one.

That change in feedback is central to the approach. The method does not assume each alternative has its own real-valued random variable from which samples can be drawn. The authors instead propose and formally analyze a general preference-based racing algorithm, then instantiate it with three ranking procedures and their associated sampling schemes.

These instantiations connect the general algorithm to concrete ways of ranking alternatives and choosing comparisons. Experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrate the approach's efficiency. The work therefore provides a framework for reliable subset selection when comparative judgments are the natural evidence, extending adaptive racing to a setting that lacks the numerical sampling model used by existing approaches.
icml-2013-top-k-selection-based-on-adapt.tldr: A preference-based racing framework selects top-k alternatives using adaptive noisy pairwise comparisons instead of numerical quality samples.

paragraphs: The paper approaches topic discovery through the geometry of how word frequencies vary across documents. Its key assumption is separability: each topic has novel words that are unique to that topic. Those words provide a route to identifying the topics from patterns in the observed document collection.

The authors' geometric insight is that maximum and minimum projected values of cross-document frequency patterns are associated with novel words. They develop algorithms using both data-dependent and random projections to identify those words and their corresponding topics. The algorithms come with provable guarantees, tying the geometric construction to topic recovery.

The sample complexity bounds are comparable to the state of the art, while the random-projection scheme's computational complexity scales linearly with the number of documents and words per document. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate qualitative and quantitative benefits. The contribution is an efficient recovery strategy whose theoretical justification depends on the stated separability condition.
icml-2013-topic-discovery-through-data-d.tldr: Under topic separability, projection-based algorithms identify topic-specific words with recovery guarantees and favorable computational scaling.
